title: Bṛhaspati Sūtra (Bārhaspatya-sūtra, Lokāyata-sūtra)
summary: The lost root text of the Lokāyata, ascribed to Bṛhaspati. Only fragments survive, quoted by others: the principles are earth, water, fire and air; their aggregate is called body, senses and objects; from them arises consciousness, like the intoxicating power (from fermenting ingredients); the person is the body qualified by consciousness; since there is no one who goes to another world, there is no other world.

attribution.scholarly: unknown author; sūtra-style fragments quoted from c. 7th c. CE

tradition.text: the time of the gods and asuras (Maitrī Up. 7.9)

scholarly.text: before c. 7th c. CE (terminus from Purandara, Jayarāśi, Kamalaśīla's quotations); lower limit unknown

structure.description: sūtras; surviving fragments quoted in the Tattvopaplavasiṃha, Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, Nyāyamañjarī, Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha and Jain works; lost commentaries by Kambalāśvatara, Purandara, Aviddhakarṇa and Udbhaṭa are cited

notes: Fragment refs (fr-…) are mnemonic labels made by this unit, not an editor's numbering; each teaching names the quoting sources.

title: Tattvopaplavasiṃha
summary: Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa's 'Lion that upsets all principles', the only surviving work of the Lokāyata current. It examines in turn the definitions of the means of knowledge given by the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists and Sāṃkhyas and argues that none can be established; the Bṛhaspati sūtra's list of four elements was stated only 'to reflect' (pratibimbana) what the world accepts, and even those 'do not stand when examined'. Worldly practice goes on unexamined; in it the fool and the wise are alike.

structure.description: continuous prose: introduction; critique of the Nyāya definition of perception; of the Mīmāṃsā 'cognition of an unknown object'; of the Buddhist 'free of conceptual construction and unerring'; of the Mīmāṃsā sūtra definition; of inference; of the other means and of Sāṃkhya. The single manuscript is incomplete.

editions.name: ed. Sukhlalji Sanghavi & R. C. Parikh, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 87, Baroda 1940 (GRETIL e-text by S. Vasudeva)
editions.licence: public domain edition; e-text for reference

title: Sarvasiddhāntasaṅgraha (Sarvadarśanasiddhāntasaṅgraha)
summary: A verse doxography ascribed to Śaṅkara that sets out the doctrines of the schools from the Lokāyata upward. Its Lokāyata section states in verse that the four elements are the only principles, that consciousness arises from them like intoxicating power, that pleasure from embraces is the human aim and pain from thorns is hell, that the lord is the king known to the world and liberation is the destruction of the body.

attribution.scholarly: a later work attributed to Śaṅkara; date uncertain

notes: Chapter numbering from memory (Lokāyata = ch. 2 after the introduction); verify. A modern Sanskrit history in sources_raw quotes the same verses under the name 'Cārvākaṣaṣṭi', a title not known to this unit from any old source.

title: Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha
summary: U33 contribution: its first chapter, the Cārvāka-darśana, is the fullest classical summary of the Lokāyata — the four elements, consciousness from the elements like intoxicating power, the self as the body qualified by consciousness, pleasure as the only aim, perception as the only means of knowledge (with a long critique of invariable concomitance), svabhāva as the cause of variety, and a closing series of verses ascribed to Bṛhaspati against sacrifice, funeral offerings and the Veda.

title: Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (Haribhadra)
summary: Haribhadra's short verse survey of the six systems (Buddhist, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Jain, Vaiśeṣika, Jaiminīya) with the Lokāyata added at the end (since some count Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika as one). The Lokāyata verses state that there is no soul, no release, no merit or demerit; that the world extends only as far as the senses reach ('see the wolf's footprint, my dear'); that one should eat and drink since what is past does not return; and that consciousness arises from the four elements like intoxication from the ingredients of liquor.

structure.description: 87 verses; Lokāyata section at the end (c. vv. 80–87)

notes: Verse numbers from memory; verify. Distinct from src:saddarsanasamuccaya-rajasekhara.

title: Tarkarahasyadīpikā
summary: Guṇaratna's large commentary on Haribhadra's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya; in its Lokāyata section it explains the names Cārvāka (those who 'chew up' merit, demerit and the unseen), Lokāyata and Bārhaspatya and expands the arguments of the verses.

title: Tattvasaṅgraha of Śāntarakṣita
summary: U33 contribution: the chapter 'Examination of the Lokāyata' (Lokāyataparīkṣā, vv. 1857–1964) states the materialist case — no continuing entity, hence no other world; consciousness from particular elements like the power of fermented liquor; Kambalāśvatara's 'cognition from the body alone, sustained by the breaths' — and refutes it to establish beginningless mental continuity and rebirth. Vv. 1456 ff. and 1481–82 answer those who deny inference.

title: Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā
summary: Kamalaśīla's commentary on Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha. It preserves Lokāyata fragments: Purandara's statement that the Cārvākas accept inference as known in the world and reject only inference that goes beyond the worldly path; the sūtras 'tatsamudāye viṣayendriyasañjñā' and Kambalāśvatara's 'kāyād eva'; and it names the deniers of inference as 'Bārhaspatyas and others'.

title: Nyāyamañjarī
summary: U33 contribution: Jayanta reports three grades of Cārvāka — the old Cārvāka teachers who held consciousness of the elements; the 'rogue Cārvāka' (cārvāka-dhūrta) who, promising to explain the principles, explained only that the number and definitions of the means of knowledge cannot be fixed; and the 'well-educated Cārvākas' (suśikṣita-cārvāka) who accept a single knower lasting as long as the body but deny that it survives the body.

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: U33 contribution: on BS 3.3.53–54 Śaṅkara states the Lokāyatika view that the self is the body alone — consciousness, though not seen in the elements singly or together, arises in them when transformed into a body, like intoxicating power; the person is the body qualified by consciousness — and refutes it.

title: Prabodhacandrodaya
summary: U33 contribution: in Act 2 the character Cārvāka, servant of King Great Delusion, instructs his pupil in the Lokāyata: perception is the only means of knowledge, the elements are the only principles, wealth and pleasure are the human aims, the elements themselves become conscious, there is no other world, death is release; Great Delusion says Bṛhaspati composed the doctrine and gave it to Cārvāka.

title: Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra
summary: U33 contribution: 1.2.4–5 reports the Bārhaspatyas' view that the sciences are only two, economics and government, the triple Veda being 'a mere cover for one who knows the ways of the world'; 1.2.10 names Lokāyata with Sāṃkhya and Yoga as ānvīkṣikī; 3.20.16 fines whoever feeds Śākya, Ājīvaka and other śūdra renunciants at rites for gods and ancestors.

title: Mahābhārata
summary: U33 contribution: Śāntiparvan 12.39.22–47 tells of Cārvāka, a rākṣasa disguised as a mendicant and friend of Duryodhana, who denounces Yudhiṣṭhira as a kinslayer and is burnt by the brāhmaṇas' angry 'hum'; the epic gives him no doctrine.

title: Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya
summary: U33 contribution: in the discussion under Pāṇini 2.4.12 Patañjali gives 'śramaṇabrāhmaṇam' as the example of a dvandva of beings 'whose enmity is perpetual' (P 2.4.9), alongside crow-and-owl and dog-and-jackal.

title: Prasannapadā
summary: U33 contribution: on MMK 18.6 Candrakīrti says the Lokāyatikas, seeing no self that passes to another world, 'taught' non-self in a wrong way, and quotes their verse 'the person is only as much as falls within the range of the senses'.

title: Sāmaññaphala Sutta
summary: King Ajātasattu asks the Buddha what visible fruit the ascetic life has, after asking the six famous teachers — Pūraṇa Kassapa (non-action), Makkhali Gosāla (purification through transmigration), Ajita Kesakambalī (annihilation), Pakudha Kaccāyana (seven unmade bodies), Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (fourfold restraint) and Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta (evasion) — each of whom answered off the point. The Buddha then sets out the fruits of the homeless life from the honour paid to a slave who goes forth up to the ending of the defilements.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Shamenguo jing 沙門果經 (Dīrgha-āgama 27)
summary: The Chinese Dīrgha-āgama parallel of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta (T 1, no. 27, fasc. 17), in which King Ajātaśatru reports the answers of the six heterodox teachers (liushi waidao 六師外道) before hearing the Buddha. The six and their doctrines broadly parallel DN 2; the wording differs.
notes: Not checked: the CBETA volume T01 is not in sources_raw. Scholars report that some doctrines are assigned to different teachers in the Chinese and Sanskrit versions; this unit could not verify which, so no teaching entries are made. Other parallels: T 22 Jizhi guo jing 寂志果經; Ekottarika-āgama 43.7; the Sanskrit Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Saṅghabhedavastu.

title: Jizhi guo jing 寂志果經 (T 22)
summary: An independent Chinese translation parallel to the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, including the six teachers' doctrines.
notes: Existence recalled; content not checked locally.

title: Apaṇṇaka Sutta
summary: The Buddha gives the brahmin householders of Sālā an 'incontrovertible teaching': against the doctrines that there is no gift or other world (natthika), no fruit of action (akiriya), no cause (ahetuka), no formless attainments and no cessation of existence, he shows that the opposite view is the safer wager in either case.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Sandaka Sutta
summary: Ānanda teaches the wanderer Sandaka four ways that negate the holy life (the doctrines later tied to Ajita, Pūraṇa, Gosāla and Pakudha) and four unreliable holy lives (the teacher who claims constant omniscience, the oral transmitter, the reasoner, the dull one); Sandaka remarks that the Ājīvakas recognize only three who have made an end: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Tevijjavacchagotta Sutta
summary: The Buddha tells Vacchagotta that in ninety-one aeons he recalls only one Ājīvaka who went to heaven, and he taught the efficacy of deeds.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Mahāsaccaka Sutta
summary: Saccaka describes the 'development of the body' of Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla — naked austerities and eating at long intervals — and says he has debated the six teachers, who all evaded; the Buddha recounts his own extreme austerities and their abandonment.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta
summary: The wanderer Sakuludāyī reports a debate among ascetics about which of the famous teachers is honoured by his disciples; the six are said not to be, the Buddha is.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Chaḷabhijāti Sutta
summary: Ānanda reports Pūraṇa Kassapa's six classes of birth — black, blue, red, yellow, white and supremely white, the last being Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla; the Buddha sets out his own six classes of dark and bright birth and deed.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Kesakambala Sutta
summary: As a hair-blanket is the worst of woven cloths, so Makkhali's doctrine that there is no deed, no action, no energy is the worst of the ascetics' doctrines; all Buddhas teach deeds, action and energy.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Titthāyatana Sutta
summary: Three sectarian tenets that end in inaction: that all experience is due to past deeds, to God's creation, or to no cause at all.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Attakārī Sutta
summary: To a brahmin who holds that one does not act by one's own or another's doing, the Buddha points to the elements of initiative, persistence and exertion.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Mahāli Sutta (SN 22.60)
summary: Mahāli the Licchavi reports Pūraṇa Kassapa's view that there is no cause for the defilement or purification of beings; the Buddha explains the causes through the aggregates.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Abhaya Sutta (SN 46.56)
summary: Prince Abhaya reports Pūraṇa Kassapa's view that there is no cause for knowing and seeing or for not knowing and seeing; the Buddha answers with the hindrances and the awakening factors.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Diṭṭhi Saṃyutta
summary: The 'connected discourses on views' (SN 24): each wrong view, including the four doctrines of DN 2, arises because form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness exist and are grasped.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Nānātitthiyasāvaka Sutta
summary: Deities who had been disciples of rival teachers praise Pūraṇa, Makkhali, the Nigaṇṭha and Pakudha in verse; Māra, possessing one of them, praises austerity and heaven; the Buddha exposes him.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Dahara Sutta
summary: King Pasenadi says that the six famous teachers, when asked, did not claim full awakening; the Buddha answers with the four things not to be despised for their youth.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Kutūhalasālā Sutta
summary: Vacchagotta reports a discussion in the debating hall: each of the six teachers declares where his dead disciples are reborn, even the highest; the Buddha does not so declare of the highest, and speaks of rebirth fuelled by grasping and craving.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Sabhiya Sutta
summary: The wanderer Sabhiya puts a deity's questions to the six famous teachers, who are stumped and angry; the Buddha answers them.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Pāyāsi Sutta
summary: The chieftain Pāyāsi holds that there is no other world, no spontaneously born beings and no fruit of good and bad deeds, and defends it with arguments and experiments on condemned criminals; Kumāra Kassapa answers each with a simile until Pāyāsi, admitting he had resisted from stubbornness, takes refuge.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Avijjāpaccayā Sutta
summary: The view 'the soul is the body' and the view 'the soul is one thing, the body another' both make the holy life impossible; the Tathāgata teaches by the middle, dependent origination.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Devadaha Sutta
summary: The Buddha examines the Nigaṇṭhas' doctrine that all experience is due to past deeds, to be worn away by austerity, and also rejects explanations by God's creation, circumstance, class of birth and present effort alone.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (MN 12)
summary: The Buddha recounts the austerities he practised and rejects the doctrines of 'some ascetics and brahmins' that purity comes from food, from transmigration (saṃsāra), from rebirth, from an abode, from sacrifice or from fire-worship.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Kassapasīhanāda Sutta
summary: The naked ascetic Kassapa lists the austerities of the acelakas; the Buddha answers that without accomplishment in ethics, mind and wisdom none of them makes one an ascetic or brāhmaṇa.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Kukkuravatika Sutta
summary: Puṇṇa the cow-duty ascetic and Seniya the naked dog-duty ascetic ask about each other's destiny; the Buddha says the observance, if perfected, leads to rebirth among dogs or cattle, and if joined with wrong view to hell.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Ariyapariyesana Sutta
summary: U33 contribution: on the road from Bodhgayā the newly awakened Buddha meets the Ājīvaka Upaka, who asks whose teaching he follows; hearing the claim of full awakening, Upaka says 'may it be so', shakes his head and takes another road.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta
summary: U33 contribution: the wanderer Subhadda asks whether the six famous teachers have direct knowledge; the Buddha sets the question aside and says that where the noble eightfold path is not found there are no true ascetics.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka
summary: King Aṅgati of Videha consults the naked ascetic Guṇa of the Kassapa clan, who teaches that there is no fruit of right conduct, no other world, no teacher, no strength or energy, that beings are fixed like the stern-rope of a boat, that seven eternal bodies cannot be cut, and that all are purified by transmigration in 84 great aeons; the king gives up his duties until his daughter Rujā and the Brahmā Nārada correct him.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text. Verse segment numbers are SuttaCentral's.

title: Bhūridatta Jātaka
summary: U33 contribution: the nāga Bhūridatta (the Bodhisatta) refutes the brāhmaṇa Ariṭṭha's claims for fire-worship, animal sacrifice, caste by birth and a creator Brahmā: if Brahmā is lord of the world, why did he make it unhappy and unjust?
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text. Verse segment numbers are SuttaCentral's.

title: Milindapañha
summary: U33 contribution: in the introductory narrative King Milinda questions the six famous teachers — Pūraṇa Kassapa says the earth protects the world; Makkhali Gosāla says there are no good and bad deeds and that each class is reborn as the same class — and finds them unable to answer.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā
summary: The commentary on the Dhammapada with its story for each verse; the story of the Twin Miracle at Sāvatthī tells how the rival teachers were confounded and Pūraṇa Kassapa drowned himself.
notes: Story location (vagga 14, story 2, on Dhp 181) from memory.

title: Sumaṅgalavilāsinī
summary: Buddhaghosa's commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya; on DN 2 it explains the names of the six teachers and glosses Makkhali's lists, including the 'eight stages of a person'.

title: Divyāvadāna
summary: A Sanskrit collection of Buddhist legends. The Prātihārya-sūtra tells of the six tīrthika teachers challenging the Buddha to a contest of wonders at Śrāvastī and of Pūraṇa's suicide by drowning; the Aśoka cycle tells of an Ājīvika who foretold Aśoka's kingship and of the killing of Ājīvikas at Puṇḍravardhana.
notes: Chapter numbers (12 Prātihārya; 26–28 Aśoka cycle) from memory; the Puṇḍravardhana story's wording (Nirgrantha vs Ājīvika) differs between versions — verify.

title: The edicts of Aśoka
summary: Aśoka's rock and pillar inscriptions (3rd c. BCE). Rock Edict 12 urges honour to all sects and restraint of speech in praising one's own; Rock Edict 13 says there is no land except among the Greeks where brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas are not found; Pillar Edict 7 appoints the dhamma-mahāmātras to the affairs of the Saṅgha, the brāhmaṇas, the Ājīvikas, the Nigaṇṭhas and other sects.

title: Barābar cave inscriptions of Aśoka
summary: Short dedicatory inscriptions in the Barābar hills (Bihar) recording that King Piyadasi gave the Nigrodha cave and the cave in the Khalatika hill to the Ājīvikas in his 12th regnal year, and a further cave in his 19th; the word 'Ājīvikehi' was later chiselled out in places.

scholarly.text: c. 257 and 250 BCE (12th and 19th regnal years)

notes: Scholarly metadata only: records donations, teaches nothing. The defacement is reported by epigraphists.

title: Nāgārjunī cave inscriptions of Daśaratha
summary: Dedicatory inscriptions of Daśaratha 'beloved of the gods', Aśoka's grandson, giving the Gopikā, Vahiyakā and Vadathikā caves to 'the venerable Ājīvikas' as dwellings for the rainy season, 'as long as moon and sun endure'.
notes: Scholarly metadata only; cave names from memory.

title: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Viyāhapaṇṇatti)
summary: U33 contribution: book (śataka) 15 is the Jain life of Gosāla Maṅkhaliputta: his birth in a cowshed, six years with Mahāvīra, the sesame plant and the doctrine of reanimation, his gaining of the fiery power (tejoleśyā) and of the eightfold prognostication, his claim to be a Jina, the confrontation at Sāvatthī in which he burns two monks and his fire turns back on him, his death in delirium with the 'eight finalities', his repentance and Mahāvīra's prophecy of his future births and final liberation.
notes: Not available locally; from memory.

title: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ)
summary: The seventh aṅga of the Jain canon: ten exemplary lay followers of Mahāvīra. In ch. 6 the layman Kuṇḍakoliya refutes a god who praises Gosāla's doctrine that there is no exertion and all is fixed; in ch. 7 the Ājīvika potter Saddālaputta of Polāsapura is won over by Mahāvīra's question about who makes his pots, and resists Gosāla's attempt to win him back.
notes: Not available locally; from memory.

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Sūyagaḍa)
summary: U33 contribution: the second aṅga is the Jain canon's main report of rival doctrines. Book 1 ch. 1 reviews the five-element view, the one-self view, the view that soul and body are the same, the non-agent self, the five elements with the self as sixth, the Buddhist momentary aggregates, fixed destiny (saṅgatiya), ignorance (annāṇa), the kiriyāvāda of intention, and the creation views; ch. 12 names the four 'assemblies' of disputants (kiriya, akiriya, viṇaya, annāṇa). Book 2 ch. 1 (the lotus) and ch. 6 (Ārdraka's debates with Gosāla, the Buddhists, brāhmaṇas and elephant-ascetics) continue the review.

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga-niryukti
summary: The verse commentary (niryukti) on the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, ascribed to Bhadrabāhu; on the Samavasaraṇa chapter it gives the count of rival views: 180 kriyāvādins, 84 akriyāvādins, 67 ajñānikas and 32 vainayikas — 363 in all.

attribution.scholarly: a later Bhadrabāhu; c. 5th–6th c. CE

notes: The gāthā 'asiyasayaṃ kiriyāṇaṃ …' was checked as quoted in the Abhidhāna-rājendra; its verse number in the niryukti is not recalled (chapter-level ref).

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga-vṛtti of Śīlāṅka
summary: Śīlāṅka's Sanskrit commentary on the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, which derives the 363 rival views combinatorially and explains each class, including the ajñānika's maxim that ignorance is better.
notes: The derivation was checked as reproduced in the Abhidhāna-rājendra (which may also draw on Abhayadeva's commentary on the Sthānāṅga).

title: Isibhāsiyāiṃ (Ṛṣibhāṣitāni)
summary: 'Sayings of the seers': 45 short chapters of teachings ascribed to sages, many of them non-Jain (Nārada, Yājñavalkya, Sāriputta, Mahākāsava, Maṅkhaliputta and others), each called 'an arhat seer'. Ch. 11 gives a teaching of Maṅkhaliputta on the steadfast protector (tāyin) who is not moved; ch. 20 (Ukkala) classifies five kinds of 'ukkala' who cut off the doctrine of the soul and states the materialist view of the self bounded by the skin.

editions.name: GRETIL e-text (after W. Schubring's edition)
editions.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

scholarly.text: among the older Jain texts (c. 3rd–1st c. BCE, debated)

title: Rājapraśnīya (Rāyapaseṇaijja)
summary: An upāṅga of the Jain canon. Its second part is the dialogue of the monk Kesi Kumāra (of Pārśva's line) with King Paesi (Pradeśin) of Seyaviyā, who holds that soul and body are the same and supports it with experiments on criminals; Kesi answers with similes, the king converts, is poisoned by his queen, and becomes the god Sūriyābha.
notes: Not available locally; from memory. Closely parallel to the Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23).

title: Sthānāṅga (Ṭhāṇaṃga)
summary: The third aṅga, arranged by numbers. Its fours include the four assemblies of disputants (kiriyāvādī, akiriyāvādī, annāṇiyavādī, veṇaiyavādī) and four kinds of Ājīvika austerity.
notes: Not available locally; the Ājīvika austerity list is recalled with low confidence.

title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
summary: U33 contribution: 9.44 — a fool's month-long fasts are not worth a sixteenth of well-taught dharma; 23 — Kesi and Goyama reconcile Pārśva's fourfold restraint (cāujjāma) with Mahāvīra's five vows; 25.31–33 — one is not a śramaṇa by shaving but by equanimity (samayā), a brāhmaṇa by celibacy, a muni by knowledge, a tāpasa by austerity.

editions.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

title: Sanmati-tarka (Sammaïsutta)
summary: U33 contribution: 3.53 — time, own-nature, destiny (niyati), former deeds and human effort, taken one-sidedly as the cause, are false views; taken together they are right view.
notes: Gāthā wording checked as quoted in the Abhidhāna-rājendra; the number 3.53 is from memory.

title: Sarvārthasiddhi
summary: U33 contribution: on Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.1 Pūjyapāda divides wrong faith (mithyādarśana) into the four kinds of rival doctrine (kriyāvāda, akriyāvāda, ajñānika, vainayika) and alternatively into five: one-sided, perverse, doubting, 'humble' (vainayika) and ignorant (ajñānika).

title: Tattvārtha-rājavārttika
summary: U33 contribution: on Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.1 Akalaṅka enumerates the 363 rival views and attaches names of teachers to each class.
notes: The names Akalaṅka lists are not recalled reliably and are not given here (gap).

title: Maṇimēkalai
summary: U33 contribution: in canto 27 ('the canto in which she heard the tenets of the religious teachers') Maṇimēkalai at Vañci hears each school: the list of teachers (Bṛhaspati for the Lokāyata, Kapila, Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, Jaimini), the Vedic, Śaiva, Brahmavādin and Vaiṣṇava teachers, the Ājīvaka Pūraṇaṉ expounding 'the Maṟkali text' (life and four kinds of eternal atoms; six births ending in release in the supreme white birth; all fixed in the womb), the Nigaṇṭha, the Sāṃkhya, the Vaiśeṣika and the Bhūtavādin (Lokāyata).

title: Nīlakēci
summary: A Tamil Jain poem (one of the 'five minor epics') in which Nīlakēci, a demoness converted to the Jain faith, debates and defeats the rival schools in turn, including Buddhists, the Ājīvaka (whose teacher is Pūraṇa), Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, the Vedic ritualist and the Bhūtavādin (materialist).
notes: Not available locally; chapter names and the Pūraṇa detail from memory (reported in modern studies). U34 may own this text.

title: Civañāṉa Cittiyār (Śivajñānasiddhiyār)
summary: U33 contribution: its first part, the Parapakkam, states and refutes the rival schools, beginning with the Lōkāyatam and including the Ācīvakam among the Jain and Buddhist schools.
notes: Order and content of the Parapakkam sections from memory; verify.
